kp.k: Sandbox tests alternative delivery models and consumer-harm monitoring
kp.d: The Office describes Utah’s legal regulatory sandbox as a pilot testing non-traditional legal service delivery and novel consumer-harm monitoring, including back-end controls. Its stated purpose is to inform Utah Supreme Court regulatory decisions that increase underserved Utahns’ access to legal assistance. The document does not identify these models as AI-based or report AI-specific outcomes.
qs: The Utah legal regulatory sandbox (“Sandbox”) is a pilot project testing non-traditional models for providing legal services as well as testing novel methods of monitoring for consumer harm, including the use of back-end controls.

A goal of the Sandbox is to generate meaningful information that the Utah Supreme Court can utilize to make future policy decisions regarding the regulation of the practice of law in a manner that increases underserved Utahns’ access to legal assistance.

kp.k: Regulatory controls increased and sandbox scope narrowed
kp.d: The Office reports that regular evaluation has led to policy changes, including additional front-end controls and a narrower scope in pursuit of access-to-justice objectives. These are reported regulatory adjustments, not findings that the sandbox has improved access to justice.
qs: This ambitious project is iterative, being the first of this type of experiment in legal regulation, with regular evaluation leading to policy changes as new information is gathered.
For example, additional front-end controls have been added over time, and the scope has been narrowed in the furtherance of the Sandbox’s access-to-justice objectives.

kp.k: June metrics record participation and entry decisions
kp.d: As of June 2026, the combined regulated-entity and sandbox-entity metric is 6, with a footnote stating that 1 entity has 2 subsidiaries. Since reopening in February 2024, the Office records 50 applicants, including 8 withdrawals, plus 1 reconsideration request from a pre-reopening applicant; 2 applicants were recommended for entry and 35 denied. June brought 0 new applicants, no new recommendations and 1 new denial; 0 applicants were on hold. Recommendations are not reported as completed admissions.

kp.k: Phase 2 refocuses evidence collection on unmet legal need
kp.d: The LSI Committee plans to reassess data collection and analysis under Court guidance prioritising models with the most promise for addressing Utah’s access-to-justice gap, while addressing Supreme Court and data-team concerns. During the transition, the Office says monthly data reports are suspended in favour of an annual report reflecting new metrics and data gathered during calendar year 2025. It expects continued adjustments during the sandbox’s remaining two and a half years; these are stated plans and expectations, not demonstrated outcomes.
qs: As part of the implementation of Phase 2 of the Sandbox, the Legal Services Innovation (“LSI”) Committee will evaluate how to best collect and analyze data in a manner that advances the Court’s new guidance to focus on models with the most promise for addressing the access-to-justice gap in Utah while also addressing concerns raised by the Supreme Court and data team.
During this transition, we are suspending monthly data reports and will instead publish an annual data report that will reflect the new metrics and data gathered during calendar year 2025.

The LSI Committee expects that fine-tuning will continue in the remaining two and a half years of the Sandbox and is excited to continue to be at the forefront of exploring legal innovation and regulatory reform in collaboration with the Utah State Bar.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no explicit AI-specific claim or prediction. It describes a regulatory experiment in non-traditional legal services, with improved access to legal assistance as an objective rather than a demonstrated outcome.
pts.d: The Utah Office of Legal Services Innovation states that its Sandbox tests non-traditional service models and consumer-harm monitoring methods. It reports that evaluation has led to additional front-end controls and a narrower scope. Its stated goal is to inform future Utah Supreme Court regulatory decisions that increase access for underserved Utahns. The document does not identify any model as AI-based or attribute changes in legal services to AI.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The Office supplies administrative participation and complaint metrics, not evidence of AI's effects or demonstrated access-to-justice improvements.
pts.d: The June 2026 metrics list 6 regulated entities, with a note that one entity has two subsidiaries; 50 applicants since reopening, including 8 withdrawals, plus one request for reconsideration from an earlier applicant; 2 recommendations for entry; and 35 denials. A footnote updated on July 31 reports one complaint in May and no new complaints in June. These are program-monitoring figures. The document supplies no AI-specific performance measures, service-volume denominator, comparison group, or measured access improvement.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The metrics are dated June 2026; the policy experiment remains iterative, with further refinement expected during its stated remaining two and a half years.
pts.d: Application counts cover the period since the Sandbox reopened in February 2024. For Phase 2, the Office says the LSI Committee will reconsider data collection and analysis under the Court's guidance to prioritize models promising to address Utah's justice gap. It announces suspension of monthly data reports during that transition and an annual report covering calendar year 2025. These dates and the remaining-duration statement are reported as written; the document does not reconcile the annual-report reference with the June 2026 metrics date. No timeframe for AI-driven change is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The intended beneficiaries are underserved Utahns; participating providers and applicants face evolving regulatory controls, and the Court is intended to receive information for future policy decisions.
pts.d: The access objective concerns people facing unmet legal needs in Utah, not enterprise cost savings. Non-traditional legal-service providers are subject to entry decisions, monitoring and a narrowed program scope. The LSI Committee is responsible for refining data collection and analysis. The source identifies no AI-specific effects on lawyers, staffing, pricing or clients.
